1. `Type safety` at `44.5%` feels justified.

That is not cosmetic; it creates real `Task | null | undefined` leakage and already shows up as compiler friction. `generation_row_shape_no_longer_honest` is similar: [generationRow.ts](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/src/domains/generation/types/generationRow.ts#L8) no longer matches fields that callers actually read in [VideoItem.tsx](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/src/tools/travel-between-images/components/VideoGallery/components/VideoItem.tsx#L437). Then `unknown_prop_bag_erases_timeline_types` in [TimelineTrackContent.tsx](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/src/tools/travel-between-images/components/Timeline/TimelineContainer/components/TimelineTrackContent.tsx#L10) literally throws away structure with `Record<string, unknown>`. Those are high-value type failures, so sub-50 makes sense.

2. `Authorization consistency` at `57.4%` also feels justified, and if anything slightly generous.

There are only `3` issues, but two are real trust-boundary defects, not style drift. `delete_project_rpc_spoofable_user_id` says the SQL function in [20260129000000_add_delete_project_function.sql](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/supabase/migrations/20260129000000_add_delete_project_function.sql) is `SECURITY DEFINER` yet trusts caller-supplied `p_user_id` instead of binding to `auth.uid()`. `normalize_timeline_helper_exposes_spoofable_identity` says the same thing about the timeline helper in [20260130000000_add_timeline_normalization_rpcs.sql](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/supabase/migrations/20260130000000_add_timeline_normalization_rpcs.sql). The third issue, `task_counts_jwt_contract_drift`, is softer, but still means the docs/runtime contract disagree in [task-counts/index.ts](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/supabase/functions/task-counts/index.ts) and [auth.ts](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/supabase/functions/_shared/auth.ts). For an auth dimension, a few severe issues should hurt more than many mild ones, so high-50s is reasonable.

3. `Cross-module architecture` at `48.7%` feels right too.

This one has only `3` issues, but they’re foundational ownership problems. `shared_gallery_is_application_hub` points out that supposedly shared modules like [MediaGallery.tsx](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/src/shared/components/MediaGallery/MediaGallery.tsx), [useGalleryPageState.ts](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/src/shared/hooks/gallery/useGalleryPageState.ts), and [useGenerationsPaneController.ts](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh/src/shared/components/GenerationsPane/hooks/useGenerationsPaneController.ts) are embedding project selection, shot navigation, generation mutations, and task orchestration. `generation_task_details_bidirectional_boundary` is worse than a naming problem: `shared` imports rendered generation details from `domains`, while `domains` imports task-detail renderers from `shared`, so the boundary is literally two-way. `shared_panes_blur_feature_boundaries` then shows app panes split inconsistently between `shared` and `features`. That is exactly the kind of architecture drift that should pull the score below 50 even without a huge issue count, because each issue spans an entire subsystem.

So on those three, yes: the scores feel earned. The pattern is that the issue count is small, but the blast radius is large. If you want, I can do the same kind of pass for a dimension that feels off to you, like `Design coherence` or `API coherence`.

> AGENT

Yes. I checked the local `desloppify` source in `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify` and compared it to the installed CLI you were actually running.

This was not just historical state. It was a real `desloppify` bug or at least a fixed upstream regression in the installed CLI.

What’s intentional:
- Marking reviewed dimensions stale after resolving a review issue as `wontfix` is current designed behavior. That is implemented in [resolution.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_state/resolution.py#L42) and explicitly tested in [test_state_internal_direct.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/state/test_state_internal_direct.py#L241).

What was wrong:
- The stale `auto/initial-review` / “20 unscored dimensions” banner was not intended.
- Your installed CLI (`desloppify 0.9.4`) has an older import-sync path in [plan_sync.py](/Users/user_c042661f/.pyenv/versions/3.11.11/lib/python3.11/site-packages/desloppify/app/commands/review/importing/plan_sync.py#L64) that only re-syncs subjective queue state when there is a review-issue delta. It does not rebuild subjective clusters for assessment-only imports, so an old `auto/initial-review` cluster can survive incorrectly.
- The current source repo has the fix in [plan_sync.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/review/importing/plan_sync.py#L138): it tracks imported assessment keys, calls `sync_subjective_dimensions`, and rebuilds auto-clusters after assessment-bearing imports.
- There is also a direct regression test for exactly this in [test_review_importing_support_direct.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/commands/review/test_review_importing_support_direct.py#L452), asserting that `auto/initial-review` is removed and `auto/stale-review` is created.

So the split is:
- `needs_review_refresh` after triage decisions: intended current behavior.
- `desloppify next` still showing `auto/initial-review` after the fresh review import: real bug in the installed tool version, not just a historical artifact in your repo state.

If you want, I can update your local `desloppify` install to the current source or extract the exact upstream fix into a patch/issue summary.

**Status**

The five newly surfaced `test_coverage` items are `open` issues, not deferred ones.

I checked their exact IDs in the current `.desloppify` state. For all five:
- `status = open`
- `suppressed = false`
- not in `queue_order`
- not in any cluster tracking
- not in `plan.skipped`

So, in human terms, yes: they are backlog. But `backlog` is not a persisted per-issue status field in `desloppify`; the stored issue status is still just `open`.

Also, there are currently no deferred items anywhere in the plan. `plan.skipped` contains:
- `2168` `permanent`
- `33` `false_positive`
- `0` `temporary`

Since deferred is derived only from temporary skips, the current plan has no deferred backlog.

**Why `next` is showing them**

`desloppify next` uses the execution queue, not the backlog queue: [cmd.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/next/cmd.py#L16) [queue_policy.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/planning/queue_policy.py#L61)

Tracked plan items are collected from `queue_order`, `skipped`, overrides, cluster refs, and `subjective_defer_meta.force_visible_ids`: [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py#L255)

Then the important part: if the tracked objective slice has drained, execution mode intentionally falls back to untracked objective issues instead of pretending the cycle is done: [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py#L295)

That is why these open backlog issues are now appearing in `next`. This is current behavior, not stale install state.

One related wrinkle: the `77 planned` count in the summary is just `queue_order minus skipped`, not “77 currently visible execution items”: [queue_progress.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/helpers/queue_progress.py#L166)

**How items become deferred**

Deferred is created through `plan skip` with the default temporary kind.

- The CLI defines `plan skip` as temporary by default unless `--permanent` or `--false-positive` is passed: [parser_groups_plan_impl_sections_annotations.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/cli_support/parser_groups_plan_impl_sections_annotations.py#L27)
- `cmd_plan_skip` resolves the skip kind from those flags and calls the skip operation: [override_skip.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/override_skip.py#L179)
- `skip_items()` writes `plan["skipped"][id]` with `kind="temporary"` by default: [skip.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/skip.py#L15)
- The deferred workflow item is built only from skipped entries whose `kind` is `temporary`: [synthetic_workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py#L271)

So the short answer is: the visible items are open backlog, not deferred, and items become deferred only when they are temporarily skipped. If you want, I can patch `desloppify` so `next` labels this state more explicitly as “backlog fallback” instead of making it look like a normal planned queue.

> DEVELOPER

But in general,other items can be backlogged?

> AGENT

Yes.

In general, any open, unsuppressed issue can be “backlog” if it is not currently tracked by the living plan. That is not limited to `test_coverage`.

The rule is basically:
- `planned`: item is in `queue_order` or otherwise tracked by plan structures
- `deferred`: item is in `plan.skipped` with `kind="temporary"`
- `wontfix` / false positive: item is in `plan.skipped` with `kind="permanent"` or `kind="false_positive"`
- `backlog`: item is still open, but not tracked by the plan

That comes from the queue filtering logic:
- tracked IDs are collected from `queue_order`, `skipped`, overrides, clusters, and force-visible IDs: [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py#L255)
- backlog view is simply “items not in tracked IDs and not implicit workflow items”: [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py#L324)

So yes, `orphaned`, `structural`, `boilerplate_duplication`, `security`, `review`, or anything else can be in backlog too. The current visible examples just happen to be `test_coverage` issues.

The one nuance is that `backlog` is a queue/view concept, not a persisted issue `status` field. The stored issue still says `open`; it becomes “backlog” because of how the plan visibility filter treats it.

> DEVELOPER

which are put in by the system though?

> AGENT

If by “put in by the system” you mean “not manually chosen in the plan,” then:

- `open` issues are system-created by `scan` detectors or review import.
- `backlog` is also system-derived. It is not stored as a manual status; it means “open issue not currently tracked by the plan.” That comes from the visibility filter in [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py#L324).
- `planned` is plan-managed, so that comes from triage/queue shaping (`queue_order`, clusters, overrides), not just raw scan output: [core.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/core.py#L255).
- `deferred` is not automatic backlog. It comes from temporary skips in `plan.skipped`, usually via `desloppify plan skip <id>` without `--permanent`: [override_skip.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/plan/override_skip.py#L179) [skip.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/skip.py#L65) [synthetic_workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py#L271).
- `wontfix` / `false_positive` also come from explicit skip actions, not raw scan.

So the short version is:

- system puts issues into `open`
- system computes whether an `open` issue is effectively `backlog`
- humans/plan operations put issues into `planned`, `deferred`, `wontfix`, or `false_positive`

For your current queue head, those items are system-created `open` issues that are currently being shown as backlog-fallback execution work.

 Plan: Deferred Disposition + Unplanned Items Not Blocking Postflight
                                                                                                                                       
 Context
                                                                                                                                       
 When all active planned work drains, unplanned objective items (issues found by scanner but not tracked by the plan) currently keep
 the system stuck in PHASE_EXECUTE forever, blocking the deferred disposition checkpoint and all postflight work. Additionally, the
 deferred disposition checkpoint only offers reactivate or wontfix — there's no way to move items to backlog (remove from plan
 tracking entirely).

 Goals:
 1. Unplanned objective items stop blocking phase transitions
 2. Add "move to backlog" as a third deferred disposition option
 3. Clean up terminology

 Decisions made:
 - Keep temporary skip = deferred (no new data model)
 - Disposition checkpoint first (not auto-surface deferred items as work)
 - "Move to backlog" = remove from plan entirely (issue stays open, untracked)
 - UX copy: "move to backlog" not "postpone"

 ---
 Change 1: Unplanned objective items don't block postflight

 File: desloppify/engine/_work_queue/snapshot.py

 In build_queue_snapshot(), after computing objective_items (line 238-241), split into planned vs unplanned:

 planned_objective_items = [
     item for item in objective_items
     if item.get("id", "") in tracked_ids
 ]

 Pass planned_objective_items to _phase_for_snapshot() and _execution_items_for_phase() instead of objective_items. This means only
 planned items determine the EXECUTE phase and appear as execution work. Unplanned items go to backlog.

 Keep all_objective_items=tuple(objective_items) in the QueueSnapshot so counts and display still include everything.
 has_unplanned_objective_blockers flag stays as-is (informational).

 No changes needed to preflight.py (it uses objective_in_scope_count which still includes all items — correct for blocking review
 reruns). No changes to refresh_lifecycle.py or sync/context.py (persisted phase is a fallback; runtime phase from _phase_for_snapshot
  is authoritative).

 Change 2: Add "move to backlog" operation

 File: desloppify/engine/_plan/operations/skip.py — Add backlog_items():

 def backlog_items(plan: PlanModel, issue_ids: list[str]) -> int:
     """Remove from plan.skipped without adding to queue_order.
     Issues stay open in state but are no longer plan-tracked."""
     ensure_plan_defaults(plan)
     count = 0
     for fid in issue_ids:
         if fid in plan["skipped"]:
             plan["skipped"].pop(fid)
             count += 1
     return count

 Export through plan_ops.py facade.

 File: desloppify/app/commands/plan/override_skip.py — Add cmd_plan_backlog:

 Simple command: resolve patterns → call backlog_items() → log entry → clear postflight scan completion → save plan. No attestation
 required (this is less drastic than wontfix). Print: "Moved {count} item(s) to backlog."

 Register as desloppify plan backlog <pattern> subcommand alongside existing skip/unskip.

 Change 3: Update deferred disposition builder

 File: desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py

 In build_deferred_disposition_item():

 - Add commands:
 backlog_cmd = 'desloppify plan backlog "*"'
 subset_backlog_cmd = "desloppify plan backlog <cluster-or-id>"
 - Add to planning_tools:
 {"label": "Move a subset to backlog", "command": subset_backlog_cmd}
 - Add to decision_options:
 {"label": "Move deferred work to backlog", "command": backlog_cmd}
 - Update summary suffix: "must be reactivated, moved to backlog, or marked wontfix."

> AGENT

Yes. Claude’s plan makes more sense than my earlier one for the problem you actually described.

My earlier plan was too broad because it changed the data model and semantics of `deferred` itself. After looking through the current `desloppify` code, the real problem is narrower:

- `temporary skip` already is the current deferred mechanism
- there is already a dedicated deferred-disposition workflow item
- the bad behavior is that unplanned objective backlog keeps `snapshot.py` in execute mode, so postflight never gets a chance
- the missing capability is a third disposition: “move this out of plan tracking and leave it open in backlog”

So Claude’s plan is better because it works with the existing architecture instead of replacing it.

What I think is right in Claude’s plan:
- Changing [snapshot.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/snapshot.py) so only tracked/planned objective items drive `PHASE_EXECUTE` is the key fix.
- Keeping unplanned items in backlog rather than surfacing them in `next` matches your stated rule: backlog = not planned.
- Adding a “move to backlog” operation from the deferred-disposition checkpoint fits the current workflow well.
- Keeping deferred disposition as a checkpoint instead of auto-running deferred items is consistent with the existing design in [synthetic_workflow.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/synthetic_workflow.py#L315).

The main thing I would change in Claude’s plan:
- I do **not** agree with “No changes needed to `preflight.py` ... correct for blocking review reruns.”
- If your intended semantics are truly:
  - backlog = not planned
  - deferred = planned but later
  then review/postflight blocking should probably also distinguish planned objective work from unplanned backlog.
- Right now `preflight.py` and `SubjectiveVisibility` still treat any open objective issue as backlog/blocking, regardless of whether it is planned: [preflight.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/review/preflight.py#L123) [subjective.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/policy/subjective.py#L111) [context.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/sync/context.py#L25)
- That may be acceptable for a first pass if you only want to fix `next`, but it means the tool will still conceptually treat backlog as blocking in other places.

So my recommendation is:

- adopt Claude’s plan as the base
- make it explicit that this is a **phase-1 fix for queue execution semantics**
- decide separately whether review/triage/preflight should also stop treating unplanned backlog as blocking

If you want the minimal safe plan, I’d scope it to:
1. fix `snapshot.py` phase selection
2. add `plan backlog`
3. add the third deferred-disposition option
4. update tests around queue depletion and disposition UX

Then, optionally, do a second follow-up pass for broader “blocking policy” consistency.

> AGENT

Yes. I found the actual problem.

`desloppify next` is not showing those backlog items because install/reinstall failed or because the old fallback code is still in use. It’s happening because the current plan’s tracked execution slice has effectively gone stale, and the queue code has an explicit fallback for that case.

What’s happening in the code:

- `next` now goes through the snapshot-based path in [selection.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/selection.py#L25).
- `snapshot.py` tries to separate:
  - all open objective issues
  - planned objective issues
- It gets planned IDs from [planned_objective_ids()](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/schema/__init__.py#L280).

The critical rule is here:
- if the intersection of `all_objective_ids` and tracked plan IDs is non-empty, use that
- otherwise, fall back to `all_objective_ids`

That fallback is documented in code as:
- “Pre-triage (plan tracks no objective IDs): all are planned.”
- “Post-triage: only IDs the plan tracks are planned...”  
  [schema/__init__.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/schema/__init__.py#L284)

Why that fallback is triggering for your queue:
- the current `queue_order` is full of IDs that are now missing from state
- I checked the first 25 queue entries, and they are all gone from `state["issues"]`
- examples:
  - `workflow::create-plan -> missing from state`
  - many `test_coverage::...::placeholder::moduleCoverageConsolidated.test.ts -> missing from state`

So the plan still has old tracked IDs, but the current open issue inventory no longer contains those IDs. That means the tracked execution slice is effectively empty for the current state, and the helper falls back to “treat all open objective issues as planned.” Once that happens, `snapshot.py` reports:
- `phase = execute`
- `planned_objective_count = 474`
- `objective_in_scope_count = 474`

That is why `next` shows the broader open `test_coverage` backlog.

So the real bug is:

- `plan.json` contains stale tracked IDs that no longer exist in state
- `planned_objective_ids()` treats “no tracked objective IDs matched” as “pre-triage fallback to all open objective work”
- that causes `next` to surface backlog as if it were execution

This also explains the contradiction you noticed:
- queue summary says `77 planned`
- but `next` behaves like `474` items are planned

Those are coming from two different concepts:
- `77 planned` is just `queue_order minus skipped`
- execution planning in the snapshot is using the fallback rule above

So yes, I understand what’s happening now:
- this is a stale-plan-plus-fallback behavior bug
- not an install problem
- not mainly a rendering problem

The clean fix is probably one of these:
1. if the plan has any tracked IDs at all, do not fall back to all objective IDs when none match current open issues
2. or reconcile dead `queue_order` IDs out of the plan before queue building
3. ideally both

Claude’s plan is directionally right because it targets the queue depletion semantics, but this specific root cause is even narrower: the fallback in [planned_objective_ids()](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/schema/__init__.py#L280) is too aggressive when the plan exists but is stale.

If you want, I can now give you a tighter replacement plan that targets exactly this stale-plan fallback bug instead of the broader deferred redesign.

> AGENT

Yes, somewhat.

Not because the code is chaotic, but because two reasonable pieces of logic compose badly:

- `planned_objective_ids()` has a permissive fallback meant for true pre-triage
- the plan can retain dead `queue_order` IDs after state changes
- when those meet, stale tracked state is silently reinterpreted as “everything is planned”

That is a design weakness. The system is relying on an implicit inference:
- “no tracked objective IDs matched” means “the user hasn’t planned yet”

But in reality that can also mean:
- “the plan is stale”
- “tracked items were resolved/removed/rekeyed”
- “workflow items remain but objective tracked items are gone”

That ambiguity should have been modeled explicitly. So the poor engineering is mostly:
- overloaded semantics
- missing invariant checks
- too-forgiving fallback behavior in a core queue function

What makes it feel more like an engineering gap than just a bug:
- the queue summary and execution behavior can disagree
- stale plan state is not surfaced clearly as an integrity problem
- the fallback hides the real issue instead of failing safe

A better design would have done one of these:
- treat “tracked exists but no live objective overlap” as a distinct stale-plan state
- prune dead tracked IDs aggressively
- or fail closed and move to postflight instead of broadening execution to all backlog

So I would call it a real design flaw, but a narrow one. It doesn’t mean the whole tool is badly engineered; it means this queue-state boundary was under-specified and the fallback was too clever.

**What Changed**

I fixed the queue bug in `desloppify` by tightening the fallback in [__init__.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_plan/schema/__init__.py). The root cause was `planned_objective_ids()` treating “no live tracked objective overlap” as if the plan were pre-triage, which broadened execution to the entire open backlog. It now only falls back to “all objective IDs are planned” when the plan has no active tracked work at all; skipped-only and synthetic-only plan state no longer trigger the stale-plan bug.

I also added regressions:
- unit coverage for the helper in [test_planned_objective_ids.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/plan/test_planned_objective_ids.py)
- a queue-level stale-plan regression in [test_queue_count_consistency.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/tests/commands/test_queue_count_consistency.py)

The underlying behavior is now what we wanted: stale mid-cycle `queue_order` residue from resolved items no longer makes `next` pretend the backlog is execution work.

**Verification**

Targeted tests passed:
- `pytest desloppify/tests/plan/test_planned_objective_ids.py -q`
- `pytest desloppify/tests/commands/test_queue_count_consistency.py -q`

- `Queue: 1 item`
- `workflow::run-scan`
- snapshot state: `phase=scan`, `planned_objective_count=0`, `objective_in_scope_count=474`

So the real-world symptom is fixed: `desloppify next` no longer surfaces the unplanned backlog there.

> DEVELOPER

so wait, why did it prompt a scan if we still have ietms behind?

> AGENT

Because `desloppify` was looking at two different notions of “queue”.

`next` uses the live execution snapshot in [snapshot.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/engine/_work_queue/snapshot.py). Right before the scan, that snapshot said:
- `planned_objective_count = 0`
- `phase = scan`
- execution head = `workflow::run-scan`

So from the execution engine’s point of view, the planned work was drained.

What made it confusing is that the summary still said `77 planned`. That count is basically raw `queue_order - skipped`, from [queue_progress.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/desloppify/desloppify/app/commands/helpers/queue_progress.py), and it was counting stale/non-live plan entries. So there were “items behind” in plan metadata, but not live planned objective items in state.

Then the scan changed state again:
- `+17` new issues
- `35` reopened
- subjective items were re-queued
- the real actionable clusters resurfaced

So the scan prompt was correct for the live queue. The misleading part was the count/summary layer, not the phase transition.

Short version:
- before scan: no live planned execution work remained
- after scan: fresh/reopened work existed, so the queue filled again

There’s probably still one follow-up UX fix worth making: have the summary show `live planned` instead of raw `queue_order`, or explicitly warn when `queue_order` contains stale entries.
